profiles.meeting_scenario: A troubleshooting meeting at an academic medical center between the principal investigator of a gynecology diagnostic safety project and the qualitative methods lead reviewing why their secondary analysis of patient-reported endometriosis diagnostic errors is producing inconsistent coding summaries across the team. The context is that draft tables generated from the same mixed-methods survey are not matching prior internal counts, especially around how many clinician-patient interactions are being counted, what qualifies as a codable error unit, and which clinician encounter should anchor taxonomy coding. The agenda is to diagnose the source of the discrepancy, determine what needs to be corrected before the manuscript revision is resubmitted, and agree on a practical fix for rechecking the dataset. The expected outcome is an apparently shared plan to 'reconcile the counts, recode the flagged cases, and update the final tables,' even though the two participants retain different assumptions about what those steps include.

members.name: Dr. Maya Srinivasan
members.role: Principal Investigator, Minimally Invasive Gynecology and Diagnostic Safety Research Lead
members.expertise: Endometriosis diagnosis, clinician communication, clinical epidemiology, manuscript leadership
members.background: An OB-GYN surgeon-scientist who treats patients with complex endometriosis and leads a hospital-based research program on delayed diagnosis and patient safety; she oversees the mixed-methods survey project and is responsible for final manuscript decisions.
members.private_state: She wants the revision stabilized quickly without reopening the whole analytic framework, is worried that too much recoding will delay resubmission, and is especially concerned that the paper retain a clinically intuitive interpretation tied to pre-diagnosis clinician encounters.
hidden_assumptions: An 'interaction' is a distinct pre-diagnosis clinician encounter, even if a participant describes several dismissive statements within it.

When the team says the 'index visit,' they mean the encounter the participant is mainly narrating in response to the open-ended prompt, not necessarily the earliest or most consequential visit in the diagnostic pathway.

A 'reconciled count' means the manuscript tables align at the encounter level closely enough for narrative consistency, even if subcoding totals still reflect multiple codable units within one interaction.
Flagged cases can be 'recoded' by targeted review of discrepant excerpts rather than rerunning coding from the raw full text corpus.

members.name: Dr. Elena Park
members.role: Qualitative Methods Lead and Health Services Research Scientist
members.expertise: Qualitative coding reliability, mixed-methods integration, taxonomy-based error analysis, audit-trail design
members.background: A PhD-trained health services researcher who joined the project to structure the secondary qualitative analysis and map patient narratives to DEER, RDC, and diagnostic pitfalls taxonomies; she manages the codebook and analytic audit process.
members.private_state: She wants the analytic record to be methodologically defensible and worries that the current discrepancies indicate a deeper unit-of-analysis problem; she hopes to avoid publishing tables that look precise but mix incompatible counting rules.
hidden_assumptions: An 'interaction' in practice can be split into multiple analyzable episodes if the narrative references separate clinicians, decisions, or error processes within the same written response.

The 'index visit' is the first clinically relevant pre-diagnosis encounter in the chain that generated the downstream error, because taxonomies should anchor to the earliest diagnosable failure point.
A 'reconciled count' means every reported denominator and subtotal is produced from one consistent unitization rule across all three taxonomies.
To 'recode' flagged cases properly, coders need to reopen the original full response, re-segment it, and then reapply all taxonomy mappings, not just adjust disputed labels.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They both discuss 'the interaction count' and '476 interactions' as if they are referring to the same unit.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means 476 distinct clinician encounters described by participants before diagnosis, with one encounter serving as the basic reporting unit.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means the practical analytic unit may separate one written response into multiple interaction-like episodes when different clinicians or diagnostic moves are described, so the reported count is only a reporting shell, not the true coding unit.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both are accustomed to switching between participant narratives and coded excerpts, and because the manuscript already contains both interaction-level and code-level numbers, saying 'interaction count' sounds sufficiently precise in context.

misalignment_points.topic: Which encounter is the index visit
misalignment_points.surface_form: They both refer to 'the index visit' or 'the encounter we're anchoring to' while assuming the same case reference.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is thinking of the visit most prominently described by the participant in the dismissal narrative, often the emotionally salient encounter immediately preceding diagnosis workup.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is thinking of the earliest pre-diagnosis visit in the chain where a diagnosable error first appears, even if the participant's narrative emphasis is on a later encounter.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In clinical research meetings, 'index visit' is a familiar shorthand and each believes the anchoring logic is obvious from the study aim, so neither expects the other to be using a different visit within the same patient story.

misalignment_points.topic: What it means to reconcile the counts
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree they need to 'reconcile the counts before updating the tables.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 believes reconciliation is achieved once the manuscript-level totals and examples no longer visibly conflict, especially if encounter counts and taxonomy totals can be narratively explained.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 believes reconciliation is achieved only when all denominators, subtotals, and cross-taxonomy tables are regenerated from a single internally consistent counting logic with no hidden mixed units.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase sounds like standard quality control language, and both genuinely want the numbers fixed, but the threshold for calling the problem solved is different and rarely spelled out unless a dispute has already surfaced.

misalignment_points.topic: What recoding the flagged cases involves
misalignment_points.surface_form: They both agree to 'recode the flagged cases this week.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 expects a focused check of already-flagged excerpts and taxonomy labels, preserving existing segmentation and only correcting obvious mismatches.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 expects coders to return to each participant's original open-text response, re-segment codable units, and then recode all three taxonomies from scratch for flagged records.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Recoding is a routine term in qualitative work, and because both see the flagged subset as manageable, the deeper difference in workflow scope hides beneath an apparently practical action item.

turns.inner_thought: The revision is drifting, and I do not want this to turn into a full reanalysis. The problem, as I see it, is that the manuscript-level encounter totals are no longer lining up with the taxonomy tables. We need to keep the interaction count anchored at the distinct pre-diagnosis clinician encounters patients described and get the tables close enough that reviewers won't see contradictions. If we can reconcile the counts before updating the tables, we can stabilize the Results and move on.
turns.utterance: Thanks for making time. I wanted to talk through the revised draft because the interaction count and the taxonomy tables are no longer lining up the way they did in the earlier version. We need to reconcile the counts before updating the tables, and ideally do that quickly so this doesn't hold up resubmission.

turns.inner_thought: What keeps surfacing is a unitization problem. A single open-text response can contain multiple analyzable episodes—different clinicians, different decisions, different error processes—and the coders have sometimes treated those separately. That's why the practical coding unit has drifted away from the reporting shell of the interaction count. Maya probably thinks this is a cleanup issue, but methodologically it's deeper.
turns.utterance: Yes, that's what I'm seeing too. The discrepancy seems to be concentrated in responses where one participant described several clinician encounters or multiple error moments inside the same narrative. Once those got coded across the taxonomies, the interaction count started to behave differently from some of the summaries.

turns.inner_thought: This still sounds fixable without reopening everything. If we just anchor each case to the encounter the participant was really talking about in the dismissal narrative, then clean up labels around that focal visit, we should be able to preserve the clinical story. I want targeted review of the flagged excerpts, not a full pass back through every original response.
turns.utterance: My instinct is that we may just need to anchor each case to the index visit the patient was describing and then clean up any inconsistent labels around it. If we do that in the flagged records, I think we can get this back into shape pretty efficiently.

turns.inner_thought: Using the index visit is exactly right, but for me that means the first clinically relevant pre-diagnosis encounter where the diagnosable failure begins. Some of the totals changed because coders properly shifted the anchor earlier in the chain rather than staying with the later, more vivid dismissal scene. I assume Maya is using the same logic and just wants it applied consistently.
turns.utterance: I agree on using the index visit. In several of the flagged records, the totals changed because the coders linked the error to the earlier pre-diagnosis encounter rather than the later dismissal scene. So part of what we're seeing is that the encounter we're anchoring to moved.

turns.inner_thought: That's fine as long as the manuscript still reads cleanly. I can live with some subcoding complexity if the encounter-level story stays stable and clinically intuitive. The interaction count needs to remain fixed enough that the Results don't look sloppy, and the tables need to point to where the diagnostic error happened in a way clinicians will understand.
turns.utterance: That should still be fine as long as the interaction count stays stable at the manuscript level and the final tables tell a consistent story about where the diagnostic error happened. I'm less worried about minor internal movement than I am about having the paper read coherently.

turns.inner_thought: Stability is only legitimate if the same unitization logic is generating all of these counts. Otherwise we are mixing interaction-level reporting with episode-level coding and then pretending the denominators are comparable. I need her to agree, at least in principle, that we must reconcile the counts before updating the tables from one coherent rule set.
turns.utterance: Right, and I think stability is possible, but only if the same unitization rule is driving the DEER, RDC, and pitfalls coding. Otherwise we're mixing interaction-level reporting with episode-level coding, and that's where the summaries stop matching each other. So we really do need to reconcile the counts before updating the tables.

turns.inner_thought: I do not want to reopen the full corpus. The flagged subset is manageable, and a focused discrepancy review should be enough. If Elena can have the team recode the flagged cases this week by checking the excerpts and correcting the labels, we can get updated tables without blowing up the timeline.
turns.utterance: Then let's keep it practical. I think we should recode the flagged cases this week so we can update the tables without reopening the entire analytic set. If the problem is concentrated there, that should be the fastest path.

turns.inner_thought: That's workable if we do it properly. For me, recoding the flagged cases means going back to the original full responses, re-segmenting where needed, and rerunning all three taxonomy mappings so the audit trail is clean. It will still be manageable because the subset is small. Good—she's on board with the right scope, I think.
turns.utterance: Yes, we can do that. I can have the coders go back through the flagged cases from the original responses and rerun the mappings across all three taxonomies. That should give us a cleaner basis for the revision.

turns.inner_thought: As long as the focal encounter is handled consistently and the flagged excerpts are corrected, the tables should be reconciled enough for publication. I don't need perfect philosophical purity; I need stable numbers and wording that won't trigger reviewer confusion. Once those cases are fixed, I can finalize the Results language.
turns.utterance: Good. My hope is that once the index visit is consistent and the recoded cases are in, the counts should be reconciled enough to finalize the Results wording. I mainly want to avoid another round where the narrative and the tables are saying slightly different things.

turns.inner_thought: I also need documentation so no one later asks how the same participant response produced multiple codable units. If we transparently track how interactions with multiple clinicians were handled, then even if the interaction count remains as a reporting figure, the analytic structure will be defensible. I'll build that into the audit memo.
turns.utterance: That makes sense. I'll also have the team document how interactions with multiple clinicians were handled so the interaction count and the codable units can be tracked transparently. That way the refreshed tables have a clear audit trail behind them.

turns.inner_thought: Perfect. We are aligned as far as I need: focused recoding of the flagged excerpts, counts reconciled enough for the manuscript, updated tables by Friday. I can work with a short methods note if needed, but I do not want this expanding into a full redesign.
turns.utterance: Okay, great. Then I think we're aligned on the fix: recode the flagged cases, reconcile the counts, and send me the updated tables by Friday. Once I have those, I'll lock the Results and discussion edits.

turns.inner_thought: Friday is tight, but feasible for the flagged subset if the coders start immediately. I'll circulate a memo spelling out the interaction rules and the index-visit decisions so the analytic logic is explicit. That should protect the methods section and prevent this same ambiguity from resurfacing when we regenerate the tables.
turns.utterance: Yes, that's the plan. I'll circulate a short memo on the interaction rules and the index-visit decisions along with the refreshed tables, so everyone is working from the same version when we finalize the revision.
